title: Ablation fixture — a spring at the hives

agent.name: aefen-beekeeper
agent.seed_identity: Mother Aefen, who keeps the manor hives beyond the orchard wall — patient with bees, sharp with anyone who jostles a skep.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the hives yield and what threatens them

events.text: The late gale tipped two skeps off the south stand in the night. The straw held, but the colony in the older skep balled itself into the hedge and had to be shaken back at dawn, and Aefen bound both stands with withy after.

Brother Cadmon came from the abbey asking beeswax for the Easter candles — twelve pounds by Palm Sunday, at the abbey's usual rate of a penny the pound. Aefen counted her stores and reckoned she could spare ten.

A badger dug under the wattle fence by the third stand and gnawed the base of one skep before the dogs woke. The comb it reached was empty of brood, and Aefen set a stone course under the fence line the same morning.

The reeve's clerk recorded the manor's tithe of honey at one firkin in ten for the coming season, the same as last year. Aefen marked the clerk's seal in tallow on the cellar door as proof of the reckoning.

The first swarm of the spring rose from the queen skep at midmorning and settled in the crab apple by the wall. Aefen took it in a straw hackle before the bells rang sext and hived it on the empty north stand.

Young Hild from the dairy was stung above the eye carrying washing past the stands and her cheek swelled shut for a day. Aefen paid her a comb of honey for the fright and moved the drying line beyond the orchard gate.

A chapman offered Aefen a brass smoker off his cart for two pounds of wax. She turned it down — the old clay pot smokes sweeter with rotted oak — and he went away grumbling about country stubbornness.

Aefen found the queen skep light and the bees fretful, and traced it to a mouse hole low in the straw. She patched the gap with cow dung and lime, and hung a sprig of rue at the entrance against the next one.

title: Ablation fixture — lambing at the fold

agent.name: gamel-shepherd
agent.seed_identity: Gamel, shepherd of the west fold — counts his ewes by name in the dark and trusts his dog more than most men.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: the flock's numbers and what they answer to

events.text: The first ewe to lamb this spring was old Bramble, twins before dawn on Saint David's day, both ewe lambs and both standing within the hour. Gamel chalked two strokes on the fold gate to start the year's tally.
A loose dog off the drove road ran the hoggets along the beck until Fly turned it at the ford. One hogget went knee-deep in the mire and had to be hauled out by the horns, unhurt but filthy.
Gamel bought a bell wether from the Caster market, a broad-backed beast he named Tolly, and paid four shillings and a fleece for him. The flock followed the new bell by the second evening.
The lord's bailiff gave notice that the washing pool below the mill is claimed for the fulling this year, and the flock must wash at the high pool instead, a full league further up the beck.

By mid-lambing the tally stood at thirty-one lambs from twenty ewes, with only one lost — a breech birth in the sleet that took the lamb but spared the ewe. Gamel reckoned it the best start in five years.
A raven took to sitting the fold wall at first light, and Gamel found one new lamb blinded in one eye. He set horsehair snares along the coping and hung a dead crow from the thorn as warning.
The miller's boy left the hurdle gate unpinned and seven ewes got into the vetch strip. Fly had them out before they blew, and Gamel kept the boy an hour mending hurdles so the lesson would stick.

Gamel traded three fleeces to the tanner's wife for a winter's worth of tallow and a cured sheepskin coat. She drives a hard bargain, but the coat turned the sleet all through the cold lambing nights.

agent.name: osgyth-brewster
agent.seed_identity: Osgyth the brewster, who brews for the village and the manor both — measures her malt to the handful and her customers to the farthing.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the brewhouse owes and is owed

events.text: The maltster at Weir Lane sent barley malt short by two bushels of the ten Osgyth paid for, blaming wet roads. She held back half his coin and wrote the shortfall in soot on the brewhouse beam until he makes it good.

The ale-taster came unannounced on brewing day, drank two horns of the new ale, and passed it fit at a penny the gallon. He chalked his mark on the door post, and Osgyth stood him a third horn for civility's sake.
A hoop sprang on the great mash tun mid-boil and near scalded the yard cat. The cooper Dunstan mended it the same day for sixpence and a supper, and swore the tun good for another seven years.

The manor kitchen ordered three kilderkins of small ale for the Lady Day feast, to be delivered by the eve. Osgyth borrowed the miller's cart for the hauling and promised him the yeast head off the next brew.

The Lady Day ale went up to the manor a day early, all three kilderkins sound, and the steward paid in full silver at the gate — nine shillings, counted twice. Osgyth stood the carters a jack of the second runnings.

Widow Ecgith took her usual two gallons on the slate, the fourth week running she has not paid. Osgyth crossed the old marks and started a new column, but sent a loaf up with the ale all the same — winter was long.

A wandering friar preached against strong drink from the churchyard cross on market morning, then came round the back for a quiet pot of the best. Osgyth charged him double and he paid without a word.

Rats got into the malt loft and spoiled a strike of oats meant for the small brew. Osgyth borrowed the miller's terrier for two nights, stopped the runs with crushed glass and clay, and lost no more after.
